ch02.title: Egypt
ch02.summary: A civilization built on an annual flood and organized around the afterlife: Ma'at and the weighing of the heart, the Osiris myth, mummification and the scribes, and the Amarna experiment in one god.
ch02.plateCaption: The ankh, sign of life, beneath the solar disk. An original rendering of the symbols, not a copy of a particular relief.

ch03.title: Mesopotamia
ch03.summary: The land where writing and the city began: the Enuma Elish and Marduk's ordering of chaos, the great gods and their temple-and-ziggurat cult, divination, Hammurabi's law-stele, the grim underworld, and the divine numbers and sacred encoding of a civilization that read reality as a script.

ch03.plateCaption: The eight-pointed star of Ishtar above a stepped ziggurat. An original rendering of the symbols, not a specific artifact.

ch04.title: Indus Valley
ch04.summary: The largest and most silent Bronze Age civilization: a faceless, temple-less urban world whose script has never been read, so that nearly everything about its religion — the 'proto-Shiva' seal, the mother-goddess figurines, the Great Bath — remains a genuinely open question, and an honest lesson in how much we cannot know.
ch04.plateCaption: A schematic plan after the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro — sunken tank, steps, and surrounding rooms. A diagram of the form, not an archaeological survey.

ch05.title: Early Vedic
ch05.summary: A religion of fire, sound, and memory: the Rigveda and its sibling Vedas preserved orally for three millennia, the pantheon of Indra, Agni, Soma and Varuna, the cosmic order of Rta, the fire sacrifice and the unwritten sacred word — an aniconic, temple-less faith that is also the great key to Indo-European religion.
ch05.plateCaption: Schematic plan of a falcon-shaped Vedic fire altar (śyena-citi, agnicayana), after the layered-brick descriptions in the Śrauta texts. A diagram of the form — not a photograph of an excavated altar.

ch57.title: Hittite & Anatolian
ch57.summary: The thousand gods of Hatti — the deliberately vast pantheon of a Bronze Age empire that history forgot and archaeology recovered. Hattusa and its 30,000-tablet archive; Hittite as the oldest attested Indo-European language; the absorptive pantheon of the Storm-god Tarhunna/Teshub and the Sun-goddess of Arinna; the Kumarbi Cycle’s ‘Kingship in Heaven’ (Alalu–Anu–Kumarbi–Teshub, castration and swallowing) and its descent into Hesiod’s Greek succession myth; the vanishing god Telipinu; the treaty-oath sworn on the gods (and its debated echo in the biblical covenant) and the plague prayers of Mursili; and the rock sanctuary of Yazilikaya. A symbology of the storm-god on the bull, the winged sun-disk, and the procession of gods in stone — with the Greek-myth and covenant links flagged as real but debated.
ch57.plateCaption: The winged sun-disk, emblem of Hittite kingship, above two schematic processions converging from left and right as the gods and goddesses do in the rock sanctuary of Yazılıkaya. An original diagram, not a copy of the reliefs.

ch67.title: Minoan Crete
ch67.summary: A religion with no readable scripture: the peak sanctuaries and sacred caves of Bronze Age Crete, the palaces with their pillar crypts and lustral basins, the faience ‘Snake Goddess’ and the forgeries Evans’s vision inspired, the gold rings of epiphany, bull-leaping and bull sacrifice, the contested human sacrifice at Anemospilia, and the Greek gods of Mycenaean Knossos, including the ‘Mistress of the Labyrinth’. A symbology of the double axe, the horns of consecration and the undeciphered Linear A libation formula, with the Great Goddess and the peaceful matriarchy marked as interpretations, not findings.
ch67.plateCaption: A double axe (labrys) on its shaft, set between a pair of horns of consecration, as on Minoan altars and seals. Both are recurring sacred signs whose exact meaning is inferred, not recorded. An original, interpretive drawing, not a copy of any object.

v34.title: The Pyramid Texts of Unas
v34.dated: Carved c. 2350 BCE (end of the 5th Dynasty)
v34.held: In place: the Pyramid of Unas, Saqqara, Egypt
v34.summary: The oldest large body of religious writing in the world: 283 spells carved and painted blue on the walls of a king's burial chambers under a ceiling of stars. They were meant for no living reader, and were found in 1881. They include the notorious 'Cannibal Hymn'.

v20.title: The Papyrus of Ani
v20.summary: A 24-metre Book of the Dead made for the scribe Ani at Thebes. Its judgment scene, the heart weighed against the feather of Ma'at before the Devourer, is the most famous image of the afterlife from the ancient world. Spell 125 and the 42 denials of the Negative Confession.

v43.title: The Merneptah Stele
v43.summary: A pharaoh's granite hymn of victory, found by Flinders Petrie in 1896. Of its 28 lines, one names Israel, about 3,200 years ago, the earliest certain mention of Israel anywhere. The hieroglyphs say something precise about what Israel was.

v53.title: The Rosetta Stone
v53.summary: A priestly decree honouring the boy-king Ptolemy V, carved in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. Found by French soldiers in 1799, taken by the British in 1801, and used by Thomas Young and Jean-François Champollion to crack the Egyptian script. Egypt asks for its return.

v52.title: The Ishtar Gate
v52.held: Reconstructed in the Pergamonmuseum, Berlin; panels in other museums; foundations in place at Babylon
v52.summary: Babylon's northern gate, faced with glazed blue bricks and rows of bulls and dragons, the beasts of the storm god and of Marduk. Through it ran the Processional Way of the New Year festival. Excavated by Robert Koldewey's German expedition in the early 1900s and rebuilt in Berlin.

v35.title: The Cyrus Cylinder
v35.summary: A clay barrel inscribed in Babylonian cuneiform after Cyrus of Persia took Babylon. It praises Cyrus as Marduk's chosen king and records the return of gods and peoples to their homes. It is often called the first charter of human rights, which it is not, and it is read beside the Bible's decree of Cyrus.
